page.title: Snapshots
page.description: Copy a whole tinyactors host into bytes with host.snapshot(), and run it again, in this process or another, with Host.restore.

hero.headline: Copy a whole host, and run the copy.
hero.lede: host.snapshot() copies every actor, queue, timer, value and image of a host into one Buffer. Host.restore runs it again, in this process or another.

section.heading: A snapshot holds the whole host.
section.p: It holds every segment's memory: the actors, queues, timers and the hibernated actors' records. It also holds the datamodel's sessions and values, the images, the system id and the host's time.
Rehearse a deploy on a copy: add the new image, migrate, run the clock ahead, and look.
Capture a host when something goes wrong and step through it. Start every test from one prepared world, or take a host out of the process for a while.

section.heading: The clock goes on from the snapshot's time.
section.p: This reminder is half an hour from ringing when its host is snapshotted. Restored on a new clock that reads 0, it rings 30 minutes later.

example.code: same session: true due in 30 minutes reminder: water the plants

section.p: Every session id stays the same. The clock goes on from the snapshot's time, whatever reads it: a new SimulatedClock, or the runtime's clock on another machine.
The snapshot's time is that of the snapshot() call. A timer with 6 seconds left then has 6 seconds left after the restore, however long the host was idle before.
host.now() reads that clock, so a journal of the inputs that came after a snapshot records it with each.
A replay on a restored host with a SimulatedClock moves the clock to each reading before the input: clock.increment(entry.at - host.now()).

section.heading: Restore with the options the snapshot had.
section.p: Pass Host.restore the charts, and the options the snapshot was taken with. It checks system, since the snapshot holds the system id.
The snapshot does not hold the I/O processors, the config's tick rate or the datamodel. Pass 'quickjs' again for a quickjs host.
The handlers are not in the snapshot either: give the restored host its own.
The snapshot holds its images, so pass only the charts it does not hold. An image already in it is not added again, and a new version is added as new Host adds it.

item.term: Only the same build restores it.
item.text: A snapshot holds raw memory, with a version of its layout. Host.restore refuses a snapshot of a build whose layout differs with TA_ERROR_INVALID: take a new one with the new build.
Durability is your database's job, and hibernation is how a running process keeps actors out of memory. A snapshot is a copy of the whole application, every chart version at once.

The services you run are not in the snapshot. The restored host's first turn announces each invocation that was running to the services handler you pass to Host.restore, with invocation.restored true and the same invokeid, src and params. Pass your real handlers to go on, or stand-ins for a copy that must not reach the real services. A type with no handler gives its invokers error.communication, and nothing is thrown.

item.term: Hibernated actors stay in your store.
item.text: The snapshot holds their records, not their blobs, and the restored host loads them from the store you pass it. A copy that hibernates actors needs its own copy of the store, since it writes and deletes blobs too.

item.term: Values go through the value table.
item.text: Two variables of one actor that shared one object no longer share it after a restore.

section.heading: Take a snapshot after idle().
section.p: The host must be quiescent. snapshot() throws a TinyactorsError with TA_ERROR_STATE from a handler, and during a migration.
It throws the same while an effect or a typed method's reply is unhandled, so await host.idle() first.
It throws TA_ERROR_UNSUPPORTED when an actor holds what hibernation cannot store, such as a function, Map or Date on native. The message names the variable.
Either way the host goes on. Here a log handler tries, and the program succeeds after idle():

example.code: from a handler: TA_ERROR_STATE after idle(): true

section.heading: Two million actors make a 165 MB snapshot.
section.p: tools/snapshot.mjs rehearses a deploy on a copy of a live host of two million actors. At most 1000 are resident, and the rest are in a store over SQLite.
Each resident actor has a delayed send pending, and half are paying through an invoked service that has not answered.
The tool writes the snapshot to a file, copies the store, and restores the copy with its own store and clock.
A stand-in payment service gets every payment in flight again, restored and with its amount, and declines it. The copy's own snapshot must be the same bytes.
The copy then migrates to a new version while events come, and runs its clock past the delayed sends.
Meanwhile the live host goes on with events of its own, its payments still in flight. The copy never reaches the real service.

table.caption: Two runs, each alone on the machine, 2026-11-20: an Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz, 4 CPUs, 16 GiB, Linux; Node.js 22.23.5 and Bun 1.4.1. Two million actors with 1000 resident, 200,000 events before the snapshot and 200,000 more on each host after it; then 100,000 actors all resident.

section.p: Every run passed its checks. The copy's snapshot was the same bytes, and the copy migrated every actor to version 2.
At two million, that migration made 3,688,631 loads from the copy's store.
Every sampled actor had its count, delayed send and version on both hosts. The live store held only the live host's blobs.
After every turn, no more actors were resident than the bound.
Core's region is 82 B an actor with most of them hibernated, and 490 B all resident. In a snapshot of resident actors, the native datamodel's rows take about 58 B an actor more than quickjs's state.
The logs are snapshot.log and snapshot-resident.log in tools/results/2026-11-20. The repository's published numbers rules say when to run it again.
